title: When you fail
hook: strive, and don't say "if only", say Allah decreed (Muslim)
tomorrow: she said the cruel thing. now what does she do with it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, when lonely: a pulse under two fingers, and a God nearer than that. Never alone. Today, a deadline that's already gone.

An email: the housing portal is closed. The deadline was Tuesday at noon, and Tuesday at noon you were in a hospital hallway, holding someone's coat. If only I'd set a reminder. If only I'd done it Sunday. If only. The replay runs all night, with a different ending every time, and none of the endings are real. There's a hadith in Sahih Muslim that names those two words exactly, and says something startling about them.
screen: `THE PORTAL IS CLOSED.` → `IF ONLY. IF ONLY.` → `A HADITH NAMES THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: It begins with strength, not with fate. The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak one, the Prophet ﷺ said, and in both there is good. Strive for what benefits you. Ask Allah's help. Don't give up. Then the turn: if something befalls you, don't say, if only I had done this or that. Say: Allah decreed, and what He willed, He did. For if only opens the door to the work of Satan. Notice the order. Effort comes first, and effort comes after: don't give up. The hadith isn't telling anyone to stop trying because everything is written. Qadar, God's decree, is the word for the part that already happened. What the hadith shuts is one door: the replay, arguing with a past nobody can reach, until the arguing leaves you stuck and bitter. Learning from a mistake looks forward. If only looks back and stays there. So the failure gets two sentences. About the past: Allah decreed it. About the next hour: strive for what benefits you. An email to the housing office. A spot on the waitlist. The next step is still yours.
screen: `STRIVE. ASK HELP. DON'T GIVE UP.` · `DON'T SAY: IF ONLY.` · `SAY: ALLAH DECREED.` · `THE NEXT STEP IS STILL YOURS.` · then, large: `NOT "IF ONLY".`

segments.voice: On a scrap of paper, write the if only you've been replaying, the whole sentence. Under it, write the hadith's words, qadarullah wa ma sha'a fa'al: Allah decreed, and what He willed, He did. Under that, one next thing you can still do. Keep the three lines in front of you for the rest of the sit.
screen: `YOUR 'IF ONLY', IN FULL.` · `ALLAH DECREED.` · `ONE NEXT THING.`

segments.voice: When you fail: two sentences. Allah decreed it, about the past. Strive for what benefits you, about what comes next.
Your line: not "if only". The past is decreed; the next step is still yours. Done for today.

screen: `DAY 1727 COUNTS.` → `HARD DAYS · 6 OF 14.` → `TOMORROW: SHE SAID THE CRUEL THING. NOW WHAT?`

howItsDone: When something goes wrong, many Muslims say qadarullah wa ma sha'a fa'al, Allah decreed and what He willed He did, and then turn to the next practical step, often with a du'a for help.

fork.setup: your cousin failed her driving test and keeps saying 'if only i hadn't been so nervous.' what does the hadith suggest?
options: Allah decreed it, and what He willed He did; then book the retest.
it was written, so there's no point practicing for the next one.
replay every mistake; going over it is how you get better next time.
fork.reveal: one sentence for the past, Allah decreed; one for the future, strive for what benefits you. the replay is the part the hadith closes.

original.note: Arabic: if, as in 'if only'; the word the hadith says opens the door to Satan's work (Muslim).

trapdoor: what you thought: accepting fate means giving up.
what it means: the past is decreed, so stop replaying it; the next step is still yours to strive for.
what a scholar hears: Muslim's hadith of the strong believer: strive, seek help, don't give up; 'law', if, opens the door to Satan's work.
guess: meeting a failure without the replay of 'if only'
failing because it was fated, so effort is useless
a failure that proves you weren't strong enough

notes: Muslim 2664 paraphrased in full order; confirm numbering and wording. The phrase is given as qadarullah wa ma sha'a fa'al (قدر الله وما شاء فعل); some read it qaddara Allah. Confirm the vocalization and transliteration.
The distinction 'learning from a mistake looks forward; if only looks back' is the script's framing of the hadith, not a quoted claim. Confirm.
